title: A combined segmented anode gas ionization chamber and time-of-flight detector for heavy ion elastic recoil detection analysis
abstract: A dedicated detector system for heavy ion elastic recoil detection analysis at the Tandem Laboratory of Uppsala University is presented. Benefits of combining a time-of-flight measurement with a segmented anode gas ionization chamber are demonstrated. The capability of ion species identification is improved with the present system, compared to that obtained when using a single solid state silicon detector for the full ion energy signal. The system enables separation of light elements, up to Neon, based on atomic number while signals from heavy elements such as molybdenum and tungsten are separated based on mass, to a sample depth on the order of one micrometer. The performance of the system is discussed and a selection of material analysis applications is given. Plasma-facing materials from fusion experiments, in particular metal mirrors, are used as a main example for the discussion. Marker experiments using nitrogen-15 or oxygen-18 are specific cases for which the described improved species separation and sensitivity are required. Resilience to radiation damage and significantly improved energy resolution for heavy elements at low energies are additional benefits of the gas ionization chamber over a solid state detector based system.

title: Impact of Rapid Acceleration on Beam Dynamics in the Rapid-Cycling Synchrotrons of a Muon Collider
abstract: Circular muon colliders offer a promising route to multi-TeV centre-of-mass energies with high luminosity. The baseline design for the high-energy complex includes a chain of four Rapid-Cycling Synchrotrons (RCSs) accelerating the beam from \qty{63}{\GeV} to \qty{5}{\TeV}. The chain combines a conventional synchrotron with three hybrid synchrotrons, which use fixed-field superconducting dipoles and rapidly ramped normal-conducting dipoles. The short muon lifetime (\qty{2.2}{\micro\second} in the rest frame) imposes stringent constraints on the acceleration process: achieving the target luminosity requires a muon survival rate of up to \qty{70}{\percent} throughout the acceleration chain, with the full acceleration completed in approximately \qty{10}{\milli\second}. These demanding acceleration conditions raise several beam-dynamics challenges, investigated in this work. First, the impact of the RF cavity distribution on transverse emittance growth is studied. Second, the mismatch between the discretely increasing beam energy and the continuously ramped fields of the pulsed dipoles and quadrupoles is modelled analytically, and its impact is evaluated through tracking simulations. Finally, the sensitivity of the beam trajectory, optical functions, and emittance growth to magnetic-field ramp jitter is assessed.

title: Track reconstruction with ACTAR TPC: a transfer-reaction use case
abstract: A unified framework for track reconstruction in the ACTAR Time Projection Chamber (ACTAR TPC) is presented, designed to address the specific challenges of direct-reaction and resonance-elastic scattering experiments involving exotic nuclei. The actroot software package enables efficient semi-online analysis by integrating a continuity-based clustering algorithm followed by a modular filtering procedure to reduce noise, delta-electron contamination, and track fragmentation. The software was benchmarked with experimental data taken with a secondary 20O beam delivered by the LISE3 spectrometer at GANIL. The algorithm achieves reconstruction efficiencies exceeding 90% across various event topologies. The system provides accurate particle identification and reaction-point determination, facilitating the extraction of key physical observables. These results demonstrate the framework's suitability for its application to direct reaction experiments in cubic active-target TPCs without magnetic fields.

title: Detachment dynamics and disturbance rejection in the TCV X-Point Target divertor
abstract: The X-Point Target (XPT) is an alternative divertor configuration with a secondary X-point in the divertor leg. We investigate its detachment dynamics and disturbance rejection capacity on the TCV tokamak, comparing it with a long-legged single-null (SN) divertor. We employ a system identification approach using multi-sine perturbations to D$_2$ fuelling in Ohmic L-mode scenarios and to N$_2$ seeding and electron cyclotron resonance heating (ECRH) power in auxiliary-heated L-mode scenarios, using the CIII emission front position as a proxy for the detached state evolution. For D$_2$ fuelling perturbations at 4-31 Hz, the gain of the front response at the secondary X-point is at least a factor of 3 lower than upstream of it, where the response is similar to that of the SN. This indicates that the reduced detachment sensitivity of the secondary X-point in an XPT configuration previously observed in quasi-steady state experiments, extends to control-relevant timescales as an enhanced disturbance rejection capacity. In auxiliary-heated scenarios, the CIII front in the XPT remains nearly stationary near the secondary X-point under N$_2$ seeding and ECRH power perturbations, whereas the CIII front in SN discharges responds strongly. However, due to complex SOL profiles in the region close to the secondary X-point of the XPT configuration, this reduction in CIII front response may not imply disturbance rejection of the detached state as a whole. The enhanced disturbance rejection at the secondary X-point could provide a passive buffer against disturbances, simplifying the task of exhaust controllers to maintain the detached state throughout a discharge cycle.

title: Deposition rate and energy to substrate in chopped and standard HiPIMS: identifying optimal pulse parameters
abstract: High-Power Impulse Magnetron Sputtering (HiPIMS) delivers higher ionisation of the target material at the expense of lower deposition rates than conventional magnetron sputtering. A fine optimisation of the deposition conditions is crucial for specific applications. Chopped or multi-pulse HiPIMS (segmenting pulses into shorter micropulses) has been proposed to enhance the degree of ionisation of the film-forming flux fraction while maintaining the deposition rate. This study investigates how micropulse length and the delay time between segments influence energy flux, deposition rate, and the ionised flux fraction in both chopped and standard HiPIMS. These quantities are evaluated by passive thermal probe, biasable QCM and mass spectrometer measurements at the substrate position. Deposition-averaged and pulse-averaged power is kept constant for all conditions to facilitate meaningful comparison. Results indicate that chopping the HiPIMS pulse consistently leads to higher energy flux and total deposition rate compared to standard HiPIMS at the same total pulse length, primarily due to increased ion flux. In chopped HiPIMS, increasing the delay time between micropulses beyond 30 us simultaneously improved the deposition rate and the ionised flux fraction. In comparison, standard HiPIMS, operated at higher frequencies and shorter pulse lengths, demonstrated similar performance with even higher total energy fluxes, but this can be attributed to a higher fraction of process-gas ions in the flux to the substrate, rather than to an increased ionised flux fraction of the film-forming species.

title: Comparison of models for dynamical structures of solar plasma
abstract: Possible mechanisms of generation of dynamical plasma structures are associated with the Schwarzschild criterion for convective instability and with excess energy (heat, magnetic): due to the superadiabatic temperature gradient, the overheated plasma starts to rise. In the framework of Navier-Stokes MHD equations, the complete system of equations for the full axisymmetric plasma model includes equations for the stream function, the azimuthal velocity component, the density change, the flow function of poloidal magnetic field, and the azimuthal component of the magnetic field. Within the framework of ideal hydrodynamics, the simplest plasma model is applicable to the initial stage of generation of plasma structures. In this case, rigorous analytical solutions are constructed from blocks. Within the framework of ideal hydrodynamics, some intermediate model - the refined model considers rotating plasma at the growth stage. In this case, some unidirectional differential rotation occurs. The full model studies the development of structures as rotating plasma from the very beginning to the highest development stage. The velocity field is adjusted to boundary conditions. Velocity components change in a coordinated manner. The stationary axisymmetric ambient magnetic field and its gradients have little effect on the plasma structure and velocity field. The movement structures for all models are similar. Radial flows converge towards the axis at the bottom, and there is an outflow to the periphery near the top of the plasma structure. The maximum vertical velocity component is reached at the center of the axis. Applications of these models to solar structures, including jets, are discussed.

title: Numerical Study of Two-Frequency Heating in ECR Ion Source
abstract: The two-frequency heating (TFH) method is widely used to improve the performance of electron cyclotron resonance (ECR) ion sources, yet its physical mechanisms remain insufficiently understood. In this work, the TFH regime in the DECRIS-PM ECR ion source is studied numerically using the NAM-ECRIS code. Single-frequency heating at 14.51 GHz (500 W) is compared to two-frequency heating at 14.51 GHz and 13 GHz (450 W + 50 W) at equal total power. It is found that while the global plasma parameters remain largely unchanged, the peak density of highly anisotropic electrons (E > 1 keV, Vperp/Vlong > 10) decreases by ~20% and their distribution broadens radially in the TFH regime. This reduction in electron anisotropy is attributed to the randomizing effect of the lower-frequency wave on electron gyromotion, which suppresses plasma micro-instabilities and leads to improved ion production.

title: Sub-sonic compressible magnetohydrodynamic turbulence I. Alfvénic and fast-magnetosonic injection, amplitude dependence, and compressibility effects
abstract: We investigate how sub-sonic compressible magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) turbulence properties that are relevant for cosmic-ray (CR) transport in the Galaxy are affected by the nature and amplitude of initial fluctuations, and by the plasma compressibility $β$. We perform 3D simulations of decaying compressible ideal-MHD turbulence at $1024^3$ resolution with the PLUTO code. The level of density fluctuations in fully developed turbulence is insensitive to whether this state is reached starting from Alfvénic or fast-magnetosonic perturbations. Fast-magnetosonic injection is characterized by an early phase of rapid shock dissipation, followed by a turbulence-dominated decay with a rate comparable to that of the Alfvénic case. The contribution of fast-magnetosonic fluctuations in fully developed turbulence remains relevant only when the initial injection consists exclusively of fast modes. Large-amplitude turbulence ($δB/B_0>1$) is characterized by a nearly isotropic Kolmogorov or Iroshnikov-Kraichnan spectrum for Alfvénic or fast-magnetosonic injection, respectively. At low amplitudes ($δB/B_0\ll1$), both initial Alfvénic and mixed-wave perturbations lead to strongly anisotropic turbulence with spectra $\propto k_\perp^{-5/3}$ and $\propto k_z^{-2}$ (becoming steeper at $β\gg1$), whereas fast-magnetosonic perturbations produce a turbulent state populated by shocks with a nearly isotropic $k^{-2}$ spectrum. Magnetic-field curvature and mirror structures are strongly sensitive to fluctuation amplitude and plasma $β$. The predicted -2.5 power-law scaling emerges only in the large-amplitude regime at high $β$. This work highlights that features of sub-sonic compressible MHD turbulence that may affect CR transport are sensitive to large-scale conditions and to the plasma $β$. Their effect on CR diffusion and field-line random walk is the object of Paper II.

title: Characterization of immersed SiPM arrays in liquid scintillator between room temperature and $-30\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$
abstract: Liquid scintillator detectors instrumented with distributed silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) arrays can be used in compact, topology-sensitive, and low-background experiments, but the temperature dependence of SiPMs immersed directly in the scintillation medium has not been widely characterized. We report the operation of a 125-liter linear-alkylbenzene-based liquid scintillator detector read out by 125 SiPM channels immersed in the active volume, over the range from room temperature to $-30\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. The detector response was measured with cosmic-ray muons, including stopping muons followed by their Michel-electron decay. Cooling from $+15\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ to $-30\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ reduced the SiPM dark-count rate by a factor of 13.5, increased the single-photoelectron response by 49.1%, and increased the cosmic-ray muon light yield by 16.7%. The improved photoelectron separation and baseline stability at low temperature enabled a selection of stopping-muon events, from which the effective muon lifetime was measured to be $1959\pm132\,\mathrm{ns}$, consistent with the value expected for a hydrocarbon scintillator once $μ^{-}$ capture on carbon is taken into account.

title: Dynamic Alignment or Angular Persistence?
abstract: Dynamic alignment in magnetohydrodynamic turbulence is commonly inferred from the decrease of an amplitude-weighted average of the mutual angle between Elsässer increments toward smaller separations. That decrease, however, need not imply that the increments themselves rotate toward alignment: large-angle fluctuations can simply lose more amplitude than small-angle ones. We therefore study the joint evolution of increment amplitude and mutual angle using finite-step conditional transition probabilities. In forced incompressible full MHD and in balanced strong-guide-field reduced MHD, we find that, at fixed initial angle, large-amplitude Elsässer-increment pairs undergo smaller angular changes than small-amplitude pairs, including when they begin at large angles. We call this amplitude-dependent angular persistence. Normalized amplitude moments increase toward smaller separation, while stronger amplitude weighting produces progressively smaller angular averages and stronger scale dependence, linking apparent alignment to the intermittent large-amplitude tail. In RMHD, a source-state decomposition of the Politano-Pouquet third-order moment shows that initially large-angle, high-amplitude populations contribute with the sign associated with transfer toward smaller perpendicular scales despite their comparatively small angular changes. Time-resolved full-MHD data reproduce the same amplitude ordering, and the local Elsässer advective term closely tracks the conditional dependence of both angular and amplitude changes on the initial state. These results show that the conventional dynamic-alignment diagnostic reflects the joint statistical evolution of amplitude and angle and, by itself, is not evidence for a cascade-wide dynamical rotation toward alignment.

title: Imaging the Current Distribution in Superconducting Transition-Edge Sensors with Scanning SQUID Microscopy
abstract: Transition-edge sensors (TESs) exploit the resistive transition of a superconductor to detect minute changes in temperature. While significant progress has been made in understanding the temperature- and current-dependent resistive transition in these devices, important aspects of TES behavior under bias remain unresolved. In particular, existing TES models largely neglect spatial variations in the superconducting state and current distribution arising from device geometry and proximity effects associated with the superconducting leads and normal metal features. Using scanning superconducting quantum interference device (SQUID) microscopy (SSM), we directly image local superconducting properties and transport current in two molybdenum-gold (MoAu) X-ray TES designs. We measure the local diamagnetic response to identify superconducting regions in devices voltage-biased within the transition and the Oersted field generated by the transport current to reconstruct the corresponding current distribution. We observe bias-dependent reconfigurations of the current distribution that track current-induced changes in superconducting regions, highlighting the importance of mesoscale spatial variations for TES device physics, operation, and design.

title: Characteristic Mapping Method for Vlasov-Poisson with BGK-collisions
abstract: This work presents the first steps for simulating kinetic plasmas with collisions using the characteristic mapping method (CMM). The CMM is a semi-Lagrangian method that uses the group structure of volume-preserving diffeomorphisms to efficiently represent the flow-maps of transport problems. Individual submaps can be composed to follow the flow backward in time to its initial foot point, numerically establishing the back-to-label symmetry. The novelty of the presented work is the handling of the source term by storing the Duhamel integrals of each time sub-interval, allowing efficient temporal-integration. Furthermore, we use the Lagrangian structure to avoid implicit time-stepping in the hydrodynamic regime, which is known to be stiff. We benchmark our method on the Boltzmann-BGK and Vlasov-Poisson-BGK equations and consider different test cases, the Sod shock tube problem and nonlinear Landau damping for different Knudsen numbers. We show third-order spatial and temporal convergence and illustrate the fine-scale zoom property of CMM for the bump-on-tail instability.

title: The Birth of Plasmoids: Weibel-Driven Secondary Tearing and its Suppression in Relativistic Reconnection
abstract: Plasmoids, or magnetic islands, dominate relativistic reconnection layers in kinetic simulations, yet the instability that creates them remains poorly understood. By tracking newborn islands in 2D particle-in-cell simulations of pair-plasma reconnection with magnetizations $0.1\leσ_0\le1000$, we show that plasmoids are seeded by a current-filamentation/Weibel instability driven by counter-streaming out-of-plane current carriers near primary x-lines. Measured growth rates are $\sim0.1$ times the background plasma frequency and agree with linear theory evaluated on the simulated distributions. As inflowing plasma loads the sheet away from the x-line, the current is carried by more particles and their out-of-plane drift slows. The filamentation instability shuts off once this drift becomes comparable to the momentum spread in the outflow direction, which occurs at a distance $\ell_{\rm iso}\proptoσ_0$ from the x-line. Because the unstable region extends farther at higher $σ_0$, our results account for the onset of plasmoid-dominated reconnection in the relativistic regime but predict that plasmoid formation is suppressed beyond $\sim\ell_{\rm iso}$ from primary x-lines, even in ultra-relativistic reconnection. Particle acceleration, variability, and coherent radio emission attributed to plasmoid-dominated reconnection may therefore be confined to smaller regions than previously assumed.

title: Feed-forward active magnetic shielding
abstract: Measurement of small magnetic fields requires shielding. For example, magnetoencephalography (MEG) measures small fields arising within the brain, in the presence of environmental fields several orders of magnitude larger. A common solution is passive shielding, but its cost, bulk and limited effectiveness motivate the alternative approach of active shielding, which comes in two flavours: feed-back and feed-forward. In feed-back shielding (the most common design), coils are driven from sensors that measure the corrected field. In feed-forward shielding (less common), coils are driven from sensors that measure the uncorrected field. The latter has the potential of providing better performance, but its implementation is hobbled by an inevitable coupling between coils and reference sensors. This paper describes an approach that employs a data-driven ``decoupling matrix" to suppress the coupling, enabling greater flexibility to achieve effective shielding across a wide frequency range. The method is evaluated by simulation, first using a simplified "flat world" in which the principle is clearly visualised, and then based on the more realistic geometry of a standard MEG system. Performance appears to be limited only by spatial sampling and numerical resolution. The method, which is data-driven and does not require geometric calculations, tight-tolerance fabrication, or manual calibration, is complementary with standard feed-back shielding methods. Active shielding is of particular interest in the context of a new generation of optically-pumped magnetometers (OPM), as the lower cost and reduced constraints of these new systems relative to SQUID-based systems provide an incentive to likewise reduce the cost and constraints of shielding.

title: Computational studies of giant edge islands and unpaired X-points in HSX and W7-X by manipulating coil currents
abstract: We present magnetic configurations in the Helically Symmetric eXperiment (HSX) and Wendelstein 7-X (W7-X), in which the edge magnetic structure exhibits island chains which are spatially larger than the previously reported configurations. These ``giant" island chains (with rotational transform $ι=4/3$ or $4/4$ for HSX and $ι=5/6$, $5/5$ or $5/4$ for W7-X) are obtained by reducing the coil current in main coil 6 for HSX and non-planar coil 5 for W7-X (i.e. the coil nearest the up-down symmetric cross-section $φ=36^\circ$ for W7-X and $φ=45^\circ$ for HSX). This appears a sufficient (but not necessary) condition for giant islands. The giant islands create X-point legs which transport plasma to the plasma-facing components (PFCs). In the most extreme cases, the island O-points leave the domain of the field line map and the divertor legs of the remaining ``unpaired" X-points do not close around the island. We show for W7-X, via the construction of quadratic flux-minimising surfaces, that these island size trends can mostly be interpreted as changes in magnitude of a resonant perturbation on a changing resonant ``unperturbed" magnetic surface. We use the anisotropic heat diffusion code EMC3-Lite to find ``giant island" W7-X configurations which are promising for PFC heat loads. These configurations significantly degrade the neoclassical transport performance but allow exploration of novel divertor regimes; for example, we show that the internal island pitch can be increased. This leads to favourable downstream/upstream plasma density ratios according to simple models; an attractive finding which motivates further investigation.

title: SensOFormer: Foundation Models for Particle Accelerators
abstract: Large-scale scientific facilities, such as particle accelerators, are complex systems composed of thousands of interacting components that must operate collectively to support diagnostics and control, and ensure safe, reliable operation. These facilities rely on extensive sensor networks that generate large volumes of heterogeneous, incomplete, and noisy telemetry, often sampled at different rates across subsystems. In this paper, we adopt the foundation-model paradigm to learn general-purpose sensor representations from historical accelerator data through self-supervised pretraining. We introduce SensOFormer, a denoising masked transformer with a Perceiver-style encoder-decoder architecture designed to handle variable sensor sets, accommodate heterogeneous sampling rates, and learn robust representations from noisy measurements. The model is pretrained on multiple particle-accelerator datasets and transferred to downstream tasks, including missing-data imputation, anomaly detection, cavity identification, and fault identification. Through extensive evaluations and comparisons, we demonstrate that a single self-supervised model can learn reusable representations for diverse operational tasks in large-scale scientific facilities. Project page: https://mahindrautela.github.io/sensoformer.

title: Detecting Muons with a Siemens Biograph Vision Quadra
abstract: Atmospheric muons are routinely detected with a variety of instruments, from cloud chambers to scintillation detectors. In this study, we demonstrate that atmospheric muons can also be detected with a clinical long axial field-of-view positron emission tomograph (PET). We performed a blank scan without any radioactive source, using a prototype feature that records all single crystal interactions. The energy a muon deposits in the PET crystals far exceeds the upper limit of the recorded energy range, which means muons cannot be identified through energy discrimination. Instead, we used the scanner's time-of-flight capabilities to select crossing events, i.e. pairs of high-energy single crystal events across the PET gantry whose spatial and temporal separation is consistent with a downward-going ultrarelativistic particle. Random pairings, however, cannot be rejected on an event-by-event basis. We therefore established the muon origin of the crossing events through their characteristic angular distribution. In order to account for geometry and event selection bias, we compare the measured crossing events to a Monte Carlo simulation of muons following the expected angular distribution. This confirms that the measured crossing events in the PET scanner are consistent with atmospheric muons.

title: Cryogenic performance of Silicon Photo-Multipliers at LN$_2$ temperature and at 3 K in the RES-NOVA cryostat
abstract: Silicon Photo-Multipliers (SiPMs) are semiconductor-based photodetectors that offer performance comparable to that of traditional Photo-Multiplier Tubes (PMTs), while providing several advantages, including low operating voltage, immunity to magnetic fields, compact size, and mechanical robustness. These features have led to their widespread adoption in scintillator-based detectors for both fundamental and applied physics. In recent years, there has been a growing interest in the detection of scintillation light at cryogenic temperatures in low-temperature experiments based on bolometric detectors, such as RES-NOVA and CUPID, as well as in emerging quantum applications. In the RES-NOVA experiment, radiopure PbWO$_4$ crystals are used to detect supernova neutrinos. The scintillation of PbWO$_4$ can only be evaluated at cryogenic temperatures, as the scintillation light yield is negligible at room temperature. We present measurements of the performance at cryogenic temperatures of Hamamatsu S13360-1350CS SiPMs in terms of breakdown voltage and gain, at 77~K (in a liquid nitrogen bath) and at 3~K. The cooling down to 3~K has been carried out using a Proteox LX cryostat from Oxford Instruments.

title: Influence of the Coulomb Interaction on the Radiation of a Few Body System
abstract: Understanding energy absorption in laser-plasma interactions is crucial for applications ranging from inertial confinement fusion to particle acceleration. At the most fundamental level, this energy exchange is governed by the motion of individual charged particles in the laser field. However, when multiple particles are present, their mutual Coulomb interaction can modify the dynamics and, consequently, the energy absorption. In this work, we investigate this scenario by solving the classical equations of motion for two coupled charged particles interacting with an intense laser field. Within the plasma approximation, we find that the Coulomb interaction between the electrons does not significantly affect the energy transfer during the laser-matter interaction. Additionally, we explore the role of mass asymmetry by considering the classical electron-proton interaction as a target system. Our results highlight the critical importance of mass: the proton, due to its much slower dynamics, acquires substantially less energy from the field compared to the electron, leading to a pronounced asymmetry in the energy distribution between the two species.

title: Cryogenic Optoelectronic Characterization of InGaAsP LEDs for Low-Energy Detector Calibration
abstract: We measured the emission spectra and current-voltage (IV) characteristics of commercial InGaAsP LEDs in a cryostat over a temperature range from 7 K to 300 K. At a constant operating current of 3.3 mA, the peak emission wavelength of the 1200 nm (1650 nm) LED decreased from 1202.3 +/- 0.5 nm (1665.5 +/- 0.6 nm) at 300 K to 1143.1 +/- 0.3 nm (1539.5 +/- 2.2 nm) at 7 K, demonstrating a strong temperature dependence. The cut-in voltage increased systematically with decreasing temperature, in agreement with conventional diode theory. To assess junction self-heating effects, we conducted pulsed IV measurements at different duty cycles. The extracted apparent series resistance showed a clear duty-cycle dependence, whereas the cut-in voltage remained unchanged within experimental uncertainty, indicating that self-heating primarily influenced the IV slope rather than the cut-in voltage. These results quantitatively characterize the thermal behavior of both the spectral peak and key electrical parameters, supporting the application of InGaAsP LEDs as cryogenic calibration light sources.

title: Improvement of Heat-Treated Niobium Surface by In-situ Plasma Treatment Applied to Superconducting RF Resonator
abstract: A specific heat treatment at 300 C, named medium-temperature baking (Mid-T baking) is applied to superconducting radio-frequency (SRF) accelerating cavities to improve the quality factor (Qo) at medium accelerating fields (10 to 20 MV/m). This treatment is very successful when done properly as it can reduce by almost a factor of two the power dissipations in this field range. However, surface contamination can lead to the degradation of Qo instead. Plasma-based surface treatment provides an effective approach to eliminate contaminants from the Niobium surface. In this study an insitu plasma cleaning process with argon containing 10 % O2 was performed to remove hydrocarbons from Niobium surface. The treatment was applied before and after a heat treatment at 500 C under ultra-high vacuum conditions (Mid-T baking). Changes in chemical speciation and oxide layer alteration induced by plasma processing were analyzed using insitu X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) and exsitu scanning electron microscopy (SEM). The results show that plasma treatment modifies the composition of Niobium oxides, converting a Nb2O5 layer into NbO2. Furthermore, a plasma treatment before Mid-T baking helps reduce unstable oxides such as NbxO and significantly increases the proportion of metallic Niobium at the surface. The Niobium sample treated by plasma prior to Mid-T baking showed a 53 % reduction in carbide formation. Moreover, the C1s component attributed to NbC bonds shifts toward lower binding energy, indicating the formation of a more metallic NbC phase. Whereas without plasma treatment, the higher binding energy component observed after Mid T baking is consistent with Nb2C.

title: LADA: A differential algebra-based simulation package for arbitrary-order charged-particle and light optics
abstract: LADA computes charged-particle and light-optical transfer maps by differential algebra in Python, with run-time order selection validated through order nine. It combines these established map methods with ATIMA-based stopping, straggling and scattering, the GLOBAL, CHARGE and ETACHA charge-state models, EPAX fragmentation, six-dimensional integration through measured or computed RF fields with reference-energy rebasing, and section-wise particle tracking with aperture and RF-window losses. Maps retain analytic dependence on external parameters; contraction with input moments gives beam observables and their sensitivities without particle tracking at each setting. Lattice import from COSY, MAD-X, Xsuite and MIRKO provides per-record status and comparisons with available codes. NumPy is the only required dependency. On the HHT benchmark, the optional compiled DA kernel on eight cores matches COSY in performance at orders 3 and 5 and is 1.8 and 2.9 times faster at orders 7 and 9. Applications include the SIBAF irradiation facility through CALINA, proton microscopy and beam-line studies at GSI and FAIR.

title: Self-driven beta-radiation detection through a graphene/water/silicon heterostructure
abstract: Large-volume neutrino observatories, exemplified by IceCube, exploit Cherenkov light generated by neutrino-induced charged particles in Antarctic ice, highlighting the potential of water-based media for high-energy particle detection. In $β$-decay, a neutron converts into a proton via the weak interaction, emitting an electron and an electron antineutrino. The electron constitutes the beta radiation detected in this work, while the accompanying antineutrino motivates future extensions toward neutrino detection. Here we demonstrate a complementary electrical transduction strategy using a graphene/water/silicon heterostructure that generates reversible current transients under beta irradiation at zero applied bias. Energetic electrons deposit energy in silicon, producing nonequilibrium carriers that perturb the semiconductor surface potential and electric displacement across the adjacent aqueous interface. The resulting redistribution of interfacial water polarization drives a transient compensation current, whereas carrier relaxation restores the initial polarization state and generates an opposite-polarity recovery signal. The complete irradiation-detector-electrometer system exhibits exponential rise and recovery time constants of approximately 1.0 and 3.6 ms, respectively. The response is strongly regulated by water-layer thickness and ionic composition, and the 17 beam pulses of a programmed 1 s sequence at 17 Hz are resolved individually. Integration with Ce:YAG further introduces a scintillation-mediated excitation pathway. These findings establish interfacial water polarization as a tunable, zero-bias electrical transduction mechanism for time-resolved beta-radiation monitoring and motivate future investigations of higher-energy charged particles and secondary particles relevant to neutrino detection.

title: Muography Simulations for Carbon Capture and Storage Monitoring
abstract: Muography can monitor CO2 storage through reservoir density changes, but site-scale simulations are costly: reservoirs can be deep and borehole detectors are small. We address both with two approaches. First, a two-stage workflow splits the kilometer-scale simulation: a fast code transports muons through the overburden, and a general-purpose Monte Carlo code through the reservoir and detectors. Second, a geometric filter at the source keeps only muons whose direction and position let them reach the detectors, within a margin for multiple scattering, and a range cut removes those with too little energy. Both are available in the UCMuon simulation suite for muon generation, filtering and transport. At a deep (800-1000 m) and a shallow (65 m) CO2 storage site, each approach reduces the computing time about 700-fold, and the filtered simulation gives the same hit rate as a full one, as long as the margin exceeds the muons' sideways scattering drift.

title: First-principles simulation of free-electron lasers with the Galilean electromagnetic particle-in-cell method: even harmonics of planar undulators
abstract: Free-electron laser (FEL) codes average the electron motion over the undulator period and add the radiation harmonics through on-axis coupling factors. This is accurate for the fundamental, but the even harmonics of a planar undulator, which vanish on the axis, are not modelled at all. We show that the Galilean electromagnetic particle-in-cell method (GEM-PIC), which resolves the electron motion within the undulator period and the carrier of the forward radiation field without a Courant limit, simulates FELs on two CPU cores at two to three times the cost of a time-dependent run of the averaged code GENESIS. The quasi-cylindrical code GEM-PIC-RZ reproduces the coherent spontaneous emission of a planar undulator in each azimuthal mode $m = 0$--3 to within 2\,\% of the radiation integral, and seeded amplifiers to within a few per cent of GENESIS run with the same physics. For a seeded planar FEL at 10.6\,nm it predicts 12\,MW of second-harmonic power at saturation, $1.1\times10^{-3}$ of the fundamental; this harmonic is absent from the averaged model. The unaveraged code Puffin, which has no space charge, gives a comparable level, 9 to 11\,MW for the space-charge-widened and the initial beam size, and the same transverse structure.

title: Learned Surrogates of Three-Dimensional Magnetohydrodynamic Turbulence
abstract: Three-dimensional magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) turbulence, the flow of astrophysical and fusion plasmas, is costly to simulate. We present, to our knowledge, the first learned surrogates of three-dimensional resistive MHD turbulence, and compare three standard backbones in that role: a convolutional UNet, a shifted-window transformer and a Fourier neural operator. They are trained as autoregressive emulators of decaying MHD turbulence at a resolution of $128^3$ and Reynolds numbers of 1000, 3000 and 6000, on 500 simulations per Reynolds number, each with one two-stage procedure, single steps and then short rollouts, and stopped by one rule. Over a window of about one large-eddy turnover time, the UNet and the transformer reach relative velocity errors of 0.018 to 0.053 and keep the current sheets, the enstrophy, the current density and the energy spectra of the simulation; which of the two is the more accurate depends on the Reynolds number, the UNet leading at 3000 and 6000 and the transformer at 1000. Applied with the same backbones and training procedure to two public benchmarks, the models reach the lowest error reported to date on the isotropic turbulence set of FactFormer, 39% below the best published model. On the compressible MHD set of The Well, their rollout errors are a third to a half below those of the best of The Well's baselines. They also match a 1.3 B-parameter pretrained foundation model in its rollout windows, with 20-62 times fewer parameters. The code, the configuration of every model, the evaluation scripts and the data generator with the seed of every simulation will be released upon publication.

title: LH$μ$C Concept: Energy-Frontier Antimuon-Proton Collisions at CERN
abstract: The concept of the LH$μ$C, an energy-frontier antimuon-proton collider based on the HL-LHC, is presented. After recalling why energy-frontier lepton-hadron colliders are indispensable as QCD explorers and reviewing the history of muon-proton collider proposals, two ways of realising $μp$ collisions at the LHC are compared: with muon-collider beams and with ultra-cold $μ^+$ beams as proposed for $μ$TRISTAN. For the latter, a $μ$TRISTAN-type booster and the re-use of the LHeC energy-recovery-linac tunnel are discussed; colliding 1 TeV antimuons with 7 TeV protons gives $\sqrt{s}=5.3$ TeV and peak luminosities of $8.8\times10^{33}$ and $7.2\times10^{33}$ cm$^{-2}$s$^{-1}$, respectively. The detector concept and the physics potential, including searches for colour-octet muons and R-parity-violating squarks, are discussed together with the main challenges.

title: Optimal Fan-Out and Break-Even Routing Loss in Waveguide-Integrated Ge-on-Si SPAD Arrays
abstract: Splitting a waveguide mode over several Ge-on-Si single-photon avalanche diodes (SPADs) relieves dead-time saturation but multiplies dark counts. We quantify this trade-off with the asymptotic count-based information rate, which prices dark counts and dead time in one unit and is attained by an optimally weighted moment estimator. For a non-paralyzable pixel, the information per pre-dead-time signal event peaks at a signal rate $y^*=\sqrt{D(D+1/τ)}$ with exact efficiency $(\sqrt{1+Dτ}-\sqrt{Dτ})^2$, which sets the optimal fan-out and a critical flux above which equal splitting is optimal. We then compare four routing architectures on 64 simulated 16-pixel arrays: an equal passive tree, static trees (uncalibrated, and an idealized calibration-informed benchmark), an ideal programmable tree, and a thermo-optic Mach-Zehnder interferometer (MZI) tree with 1.32 dB excess loss. Ideal programmability gains up to 15.9 dB over equal splitting at low flux. At one known flux, however, the calibrated static splitter beats the MZI tree by 0.14-2.7 dB, and the penalty tends to twice the excess loss when dark counts dominate. In ensemble-median worst-case regret, the MZI tree breaks even only for flux windows wider than 2.55 decades, and not within six decades above about 3.4 dB excess loss. Event-level Monte Carlo simulations reproduce the count statistics and the predicted estimator variances within bootstrap confidence intervals. Sensitivity analyses cover dark-count level, heterogeneity, detector model and random seed. All results are simulations with representative literature parameters.

title: Ton-scale Xenon Gas TPC for $0νββ$ Search at Atmospheric Pressure
abstract: We explore aspects of an unorthodox ton-scale xenon gas time projection chamber detector operated at normal temperature and pressure (NTP), designed for $0νββ$ discovery at $\sim10^{27}$ year sensitivity. At fixed active mass, a greater transparency to $γ$-ray backgrounds and better track clarity exists at NTP relative to higher density. Operation at NTP also alleviates difficulties with pressure containment and significantly reduces HV requirements. With metre-scale electron tracks at a few MeV, event topology can be used to efficiently reject the copious $γ$-ray backgrounds by factors ranging from 550--1200, largely compensating for the greater surface area of the detector. Event topology is captured from anode plane signals combined with sensing the secondary ion component arriving at the cathode plane. A molecular gas admixture limits diffusion of the secondary electron tracks to less than one cm rms and provides stable proportional avalanche gain for measurement of energy. An energy resolution $δ$E/E $\leq$ 1\% FWHM seems possible. A 100 kg scale demonstrator for this detector technology could lead directly to a ton-scale search.

title: Radiofrequency plasma spheroidization of lightweight complex concentrated superalloy Al10Nb20Ta15Ti30V5Zr20
abstract: Recent advances in additive manufacturing (AM) have significantly increased the demand for high-quality metal powders with tailored composition. For refractory complex concentrated alloys (RCCA) preparing such powders by conventional metallurgical method remains challenging due to their high melting point and chemical reactivity. In this paper, we present a method to produce spherical RCCA powders (here Al10Nb20Ta15Ti30V5Zr20) via mechanical alloying followed by radio-frequency inductively coupled plasma spheroidization. The resulting powder is suitable for AM processes because of its spherical morphology and a microstructure consisting of major BCC phases with local B2 phase. Complex carbide formation was studied by 3D atom probe tomography.

title: Impedance of multilayer cylindrical structures with a material-filled beam region
abstract: Beam-coupling impedances in material media are relevant for ionization-cooling channels of a future muon collider, where the beam propagates in matter rather than vacuum. We extend the cylindrical field-matching formalism for multilayer structures to the case of a material-filled beam region surrounded by external layers with arbitrary electromagnetic properties. Relative to the vacuum formulation, the usual factor $1/γ^2$ is replaced by the material-dependent factor $F=1/\varepsilon_1-μ_1β^2$, and the radial propagation constant is modified accordingly. Analytical expressions are obtained for the monopolar longitudinal and dipolar transverse impedances, with the surrounding structure encoded through reflection coefficients determined by field matching. The formalism reduces to the known vacuum and perfectly conducting limits in the appropriate cases. Representative calculations are presented for absorber-relevant configurations, illustrating the dependence on the material properties of both the beam region and the surrounding layers. In particular, a finite beam-region conductivity can generate a real impedance component and reverse the sign of the imaginary space-charge impedance, while sufficiently high permittivity can give rise to resonant structures associated with oscillatory radial fields. The effect of finite-conductivity surroundings is also examined, showing the approach towards the perfectly conducting limit as the external conductivity is increased. The applicability of the infinite-length approximation is also discussed by comparison with finite-length mode-matching results.

title: Implicit-Explicit Methods for the GX Gyrokinetics Code
abstract: Gyrokinetic simulations are crucial for understanding turbulent transport in magnetic confinement fusion devices. Unfortunately, these simulations are typically extremely expensive, particularly when kinetically evolving electrons due to their significantly greater thermal speed compared to that of ions. In this work, we present new implicit-explicit timestepping methods for the GX gyrokinetics code to accelerate these simulations where the ion and electron streaming terms as well as the electron mirror terms are treated implicitly, while the remaining terms are treated explicitly. These methods include a lower-order Lie-Trotter splitting method as well as a higher-order additive Runge-Kutta method. Our schemes take advantage of the sparsity of the GX equations, which allows us to efficiently invert the linear operators that arise from the implicit scheme without consuming significant amounts of limited GPU memory. We demonstrate our new integration scheme for both linear (electrostatic and electromagnetic) and nonlinear (electrostatic) simulations in general toroidal geometry, and show that our methods can achieve up to the maximum theoretical linearly stable timestep for these simulations while maintaining a significant improvement in wall-clock time.

title: Comments on the paper "Eliminating beam-induced depolarizing effects in the hydrogen jet target for high-precision proton beam polarimetry at the Electron-Ion Collider"
abstract: A critical review of the methodology used in F. Rathmann et al., Phys. Rev. Accel. Beams 29, 021001 (2026), to evaluate beam-induced depolarization of the Atomic Polarized Hydrogen Gas Jet (HJET) target at the Electron--Ion Collider (EIC) is presented. It is shown that several key assumptions underlying that analysis -- including the introduction of a photon emission threshold, the application of Fermi's Golden Rule to coherent hyperfine transitions, the interpretation of power broadening as a physical linewidth increase, and the treatment of spatial magnetic fields -- are either incorrect or internally inconsistent. As a consequence, the predicted large depolarization effects are demonstrated to be artifacts of the adopted methodology rather than genuine physical phenomena. A consistent quantum-mechanical treatment based on the time-dependent Schrödinger equation shows that beam-induced depolarization probabilities at the EIC are negligibly small.

title: Optical Acceptance Testing of Serenity-S1 Boards for the CMS HGCAL Phase-2 Backend Electronics
abstract: The CMS Phase-2 upgrade includes a new high-granularity calorimeter. The calorimeter electronics will include around 300 Serenity-S1 FPGA boards that use Samtec FireFly electro-optical modules with a link speed of up to 25 Gbps. General production tests performed by the central Serenity group only validate the high-speed links via copper loopback cables. We present an optical acceptance test framework specifically designed for the calorimeter, providing comprehensive link and slow-control validation of installed FireFly modules under realistic operating conditions. This test combines loopback and board-to-board testing, extended bit error ratio measurements, and continuous module health monitoring within an automated workflow, delivering structured diagnostics and ensuring reliable large-scale system deployment.

title: Ultrashort pulsed laser atmospheric filament properties and microwave radiation inferred from S-band guided wave interaction and self-emission
abstract: The electrical conductivity $σ$ of the plasma filament left behind by an ultrashort pulsed laser (USPL) optical pulse after it is geometrically then self-focused in air via the Kerr effect is measured by attenuation of a 3.2 GHz TE$_{10}$ mode within an S-band waveguide through which the filament passes, taking into account the characteristic radius $R$ of the filament, as determined by fast camera visible light imaging. Models of the major air constituents' ionization rate $W_{i}$ vs. local laser intensity $I$, and of electron temperature $T$ and mean axial electron momentum $\left\langle p_{z}\right\rangle $ vs. peak laser intensity $I_{0}$ are then used to infer a hypothetical steady state filament's $I_{0}$, $T$, major species particle densities, and assumed axially invariant current time integral $Q$ and current decay rate $ν$ after pulse passage. $Q$ is independently measured via the filament's self-emission signal in the waveguide for comparison. The theoretical far field microwave radiation pattern due to the actual axial variation in $Q=Q\left( z\right) $ is compared favorably to published measurements. A much lower upper bound on $ν$ is inferred once such radiation is taken into account. Results are presented along a $30$~cm long filament at a broad range of atmospheric pressures.

title: Sealed, Lightweight gRPC-Based Muon Telescopes for Muography Applications
abstract: Portable muon detection systems are increasingly in demand for muography applications in environments requiring flexible installation and transportability. We present the ongoing development and implementation of portable muon tracking systems based on glass Resistive Plate Chambers (gRPCs). The work addresses the fabrication and assembly of compact, position-sensitive RPC detectors, along with their performance when operated with a standard gas mixture and coupled to external front-end electronics and a scalable multi-channel data-acquisition system. The system design prioritizes modular construction, mechanical robustness, operational safety, autonomous functionality, and cost-effectiveness. Measurements with atmospheric muons demonstrated stable detector performance and reliable tracking capability, confirming the suitability of this architecture for muographic measurements. We conclude with an outlook on further developments of the detection system.

title: Bayesian optimization of longitudinally aligned CNT targets for 800 nm laser wakefield acceleration in the bubble regime
abstract: Laser wakefield acceleration (LWFA) in solid-density plasmas can reach accelerating gradients in the TeV/m range, well above those of gaseous media, provided the driver is matched to the plasma. In nanostructured solids, this matching can be achieved by controlling the spacing between the nanostructures to reduce the effective density, enabling infrared pulses to excite wakefields in the bubble regime. Following numerical demonstrations with carbon nanotube (CNT) bundles on concentric cylindrical shells, a simpler, experimentally more accessible longitudinally aligned CNT (LA-CNT) target is investigated here, with the bundles on a triangular lattice within a square cross section and an optional central aperture. Three-dimensional particle-in-cell simulations are coupled with Bayesian optimization to vary the effective density, target length, bundle radius and aperture radius for a fixed 100 mJ, few-cycle, 800 nm laser pulse, maximizing the laser-to-beam energy conversion efficiency for electrons above 20 MeV. With the aperture radius constrained to at least 0.5 $μ$m, the best target operates in the bubble regime and reaches an efficiency of 24.6%, delivering a 673 pC bunch with a mean energy of 36.6 MeV and a quasi-monoenergetic peak near 46 MeV, against 19% for the concentric-shell target under identical conditions. When the aperture is allowed to vanish, the optimization converges to denser and shorter targets, the efficiency peaks at 25.8%, and the best configurations deliver a higher charge at the cost of a lower peak energy and about 50% larger divergence; aperture-free targets among them retain a mean efficiency of 24.1%. The optimized targets are robust to random bundle displacements that preserve the effective density. By eliminating the need to pattern a micrometre-scale opening, aperture-free targets may facilitate proof-of-principle experiments on solid-state LWFA.

title: Low Frequency Noise Identification for the SuperCDMS Experiment using Convolutional Neural Networks
abstract: The SuperCDMS experiment uses semiconductor crystal detectors operated at cryogenic temperatures to search for low-mass dark matter. Vibrations observed during the SuperCDMS Soudan experiment generated broadband low-frequency noise (LFN), which due to its similarity in the pulse shape to the low-energy signal events is difficult to remove. In the final low ionization threshold analysis, CDMSlite Run 3, the strong event selection criterion applied to remove LFN events also significantly reduced the ability to identify signal events in the low energy region, thus reducing the sensitivity of the experiment to low-mass dark matter. Therefore, an LFN rejection criterion using machine learning (ML) aimed to improve the signal efficiency while maintaining the signal purity has now been developed. This paper presents a new method using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), its application to the CDMSlite Run 3 dataset, and its impact on dark matter sensitivities, with further investigation through case studies.

title: Localized anomaly detection with a calorimeter normalizing flow
abstract: Normalizing flows trained as fast calorimeter simulators also give the likelihood of each shower, which can serve as an anomaly score. Because this likelihood sums over every voxel, a signal confined to a few voxels can be lost in the fluctuations of the rest of the shower. For example, in a public benchmark dataset in which a long-lived neutral particle decays to two photons, the CaloFlow likelihood used in previous work selects less than 5% of the signal at a background efficiency of $10^{-3}$ when the particle has the largest simulated mass and decays at or just behind the front face of the calorimeter. In this work, we define a regional anomaly score by summing the squared latent coordinates of the same flow within small detector regions around the point where the particle enters the calorimeter, with the threshold set using background showers alone. At the same background efficiency, this regional anomaly score selects more than 95% of the signal. The per-coordinate likelihood terms, summed over the same regions, perform equally well, but the squared latent coordinates have a known distribution for background showers and clearly illustrate when a shower departs from it. Therefore, normalizing flows may be sensitive to new physics, even if the global likelihood is not.

title: The Equations of Reduced Magnetohydrodynamics in Dipole Coordinates
abstract: The equations of reduced magnetohydrodynamics (RMHD) isolate the Alfvénic energy transfer and turbulence dynamics from MHD in a computationally tractable way. In this study, we derive the equations of RMHD for a low $β$ plasma in a dipole coordinate system aligned with an inhomogeneous background that is general enough to represent the Earth's magnetosphere using a multiscale analysis and the Kreiss theorem. The most important effect beyond homogeneous RMHD is the propensity for background Alfvén speed gradients to drive nonlinear wave effects. This work has immediate application to the magnetosphere-ionosphere coupling problem in the Earth's magnetosphere, where the Alfvén speed varies by an order of magnitude over a short distance. We estimate the turbulent energy transfer driven by this. In Earth's magneotsphere, a substantial portion of energy ($>20\%$) could be transferred in this way along auroral field lines. A revised field aligned current density mapping technique to account for this energy loss mechanism is proposed to replace using $j_\parallel/B_0$ being constant along the field line. We also predict the existence of a ``saturation current density,'' where there is a maximum $j_\parallel$ that exist before driving a nonlinear cascade. At Earth, this value is $\sim 5\; μ\text{A}/\text{m}^2$ at the ionosphere, which corresponds to the maximum observed value by ground magnetometers. Furthermore, this study makes use of a novel methodology, a computer algebra system, in performing algebraic work under complicated coordinate systems. We hope this approach serves as a template for performing reproducible and verifiable multiscale perturbation analysis under arbitrarily complex geometries.

title: Towards reactor-relevant electromagnetic turbulence in the MAST-U spherical tokamak
abstract: We investigate electromagnetic ion-scale turbulence in a high-performing H-mode plasma of the Mega Ampere Spherical Tokamak Upgrade (MAST-U) with local gyrokinetic simulations, asking whether it approaches the non-zonal transition: the nonlinear transition to a high-flux state above a critical value of $q^{2}β_{e}$ found in simulations of STEP, where $q$ is the safety factor and $β_{e}$ the ratio of electron thermal pressure to magnetic pressure. We examine two flux surfaces: one at $t = 531\,\mathrm{ms}$, close to peak normalised pressure $β_N$, at normalised poloidal flux $ψ_N = 0.50$; and one at $t = 591\,\mathrm{ms}$ and $ψ_N = 0.60$, the ideal-ballooning-stable surface of largest $q^{2}β_e$ inside $ψ_N = 0.8$ at that time. On both surfaces the dominant ion-scale instabilities are microtearing and electromagnetic ballooning-like modes, as in STEP. Without equilibrium flow shear, at least one of the surfaces lies above the large flux threshold with every set of kinetic species we simulate, with ion-scale heat fluxes far exceeding power balance, in turbulence characterised by a highly stochastic magnetic field. Strong flow shear driven by neutral-beam injection in the real experiment suppresses this turbulence and holds the plasma below the transition. When the carbon impurity is included in the simulation, the ion-scale flux is then close to power balance on both surfaces. Without rotation, gyrokinetics suggests the transition would limit the accessible profiles. This could degrade MAST-U plasma performance using heating schemes that lack a momentum source, and this will be tested in forthcoming electron Bernstein wave heating experiments.

title: Magnetic Johnson noise from arbitrarily shaped conductors: experimental validation of the fluctuation-dissipation finite-element method
abstract: Magnetic Johnson noise--magnetic noise caused by thermal current fluctuations in conducting materials--can interfere with measurements and limit their sensitivity. As the sensitivity of experiments increases, it becomes increasingly important to accurately estimate the magnetic Johnson noise from experimental components with complex shapes during both the design and analysis phases. A particularly powerful approach is to combine the fluctuation-dissipation theorem with finite-element calculations. This versatile approach can be used to calculate the magnetic Johnson noise from conductors of arbitrary geometry for a wide range of frequencies and for magnetic field detectors with general geometries, such as a finite-sized loop or a gradiometer. Using a SQUID gradiometer array, we measured the magnetic Johnson noise from conductors with complex geometries and compared the results with calculations performed using this method. The calculations reproduce both the measured noise amplitude and its frequency dependence, providing an experimental validation of this method. We also performed a detailed analysis of how the geometry and material parameters affect the frequency dependence of magnetic Johnson noise.

title: Soft X-Ray Detection Down to the Nitrogen K-Edge Using a Pixelated iLGAD Sensor
abstract: Hybrid pixel detectors represent the state-of-the-art technology for hard X-ray experiments at synchrotron light sources and free-electron lasers, owing to their high frame rates, extended dynamic range, and scalable detection areas. However, their application in the soft X-ray regime remains bottlenecked by the challenge of developing a sensor that can achieve high quantum efficiency and an sufficient signal-to-noise ratio at low photon energies. Here, we present inverse low-gain avalanche diode (iLGAD) sensors integrated with a thin entrance window, demonstrating single-photon resolution down to 390 eV (below the Nitrogen K-edge) with a signal-to-noise ratio of 5. Two gain layer designs, standard gain layer and shallow gain layer, were systematically investigated to evaluate their spectral response as a function of photon energy and operating temperature. A double-peak feature is observed in the energy spectrum, arising from the dependence of charge multiplication on photon absorption depth. Furthermore, a phenomenological spectral fitting model was established, enabling the quantitative extraction of the effective $\mathrm{n}^+$ layer thickness and gain layer depth. Beyond providing a fundamental understanding of iLGAD charge multiplication mechanisms and characterization results in the soft X-ray regime, these findings lay the foundation for developing large-area, high-frame-rate hybrid pixel detectors for soft X-ray. This advancement directly benefits soft X-ray photon science applications, including high-resolution ptychography, spectroscopy, and resonant scattering at synchrotron and FEL beamlines.

title: Challenges in the verification of MOSAIX ASIC for ALICE ITS3
abstract: The MOSAIX is a wafer-scale, full-functionality prototype ASIC for the ALICE Inner Tracking System (ITS3) upgrade, implemented in $65\,\text{nm}$ stitching technology. It integrates 144 independently powered pixel matrices, eight $10\,\text{Gb/s}$ serializers, and on-chip data and power distribution, making full-chip verification highly resource-intensive (over $80\,\text{GB}$ of memory and 192,000 tests). Verification also targets a sophisticated power-up sequence and radiation conditions of $10^{6}$\ particles $s^{-1} cm^{-2}$ and $4\,\text{kGy}$ TID. This work presents a UVM-based verification strategy that identified 260 design errors and summarizes key lessons from ASIC sign-off.

title: Calorimetry as inference: the information content of particle showers and the limits of energy measurement
abstract: A calorimeter does not measure the energy of a particle, it infers it from the record the absorption process leaves behind. Energy conservation writes every event as an accounting ledger, E = E_dis + E_B + E_esc + E_nu, of which only the dissipated component contributes to signal, so resolution is limited by how well the record of the dissipation constrains the missing entries. We formalize this: records form a lattice on which information is monotone; thinning a Poisson record scales Fisher information exactly by the retention; clustered records read out as sums cost the 1/(1+cv^2); and the quadrature budget a/sqrt(E) (+) b is the floor of every summed readout. The "ultimate limits" of hadronic calorimetry are identified as the first rung of a ladder, the residual spread of the invisible energy around a single correlated observable. We measure the ladder above that rung on Geant4 truth records of hadronic showers in copper, from the dissipated-energy sum to time-, position- and multiplicity-resolved records, with estimators validated on exactly solvable toy models. The achieved full-record value, model-conditional, is about 5.5%/sqrt(E) (+) 0.3% over 20-100 GeV, a factor 1.7-1.9 below the canonical one-functional construction on the same events (1.29% vs. 2.14% at 20 GeV). Under retrained high-precision neutron transport it moves from 1.29% to 1.30%, the dissipated-energy sum by 7%, and the gain from time structure becomes 0.17% in place of 0.28%. Dual-readout supplies the largest share of the information. Shower shape is next, almost entirely longitudinal, saturating at about one interaction length. Time structure adds nearly as much with or without shower shape, and stopped-muon neutrino losses set an estimated floor of 0.99% at 20 GeV. Every readout dimension has a measured information exchange rate, separating what new hardware can buy from what better algorithms can recover.

title: Is Your AI Fast Enough to Run a Fusion Reactor?
abstract: In magnetic confinement fusion, compact machine learning algorithms are often integrated into the control loop on CPU-based custom hardware stacks. Deterministic implementations of these algorithms target instabilities which can evolve over microseconds to milliseconds. Staying within this framework may therefore limit the pace of control-system development to the inference time available. With the expansion of hardware acceleration and large models, we aim to bring ML models for fusion control to modern inference engines and compare, based on the physics reactor, the suitability of each engine per model. This study implements a consistent real-time machine learning algorithm for GPUs and optimized CPU packages, including OpenVINO, XLA, and TVM, at DIII-D National Fusion Facility. For the smallest model, one CPU core responds within 3.6 $μ$s in 99% of control cycles and an NVIDIA A100 within 28 $μ$s. We also evaluate models running simultaneously, as they would run in a typical experiment, and find best use cases per framework.

title: Commutative Coarse-graining on the Sphere
abstract: Filtering by spatial convolution underlies coarse-graining and Large Eddy Simulation, the analysis of multiscale dynamics, and data processing across the sciences. Yet, as commonly practiced on the sphere, it violates a basic consistency requirement: commutation with differential operators, which is necessary for deriving coarse-grained dynamics and preserving the physics across lengthscales. The root of the problem is nonlocality of filtering, which compares directions in different tangent planes. The same reason underlies the Foucault pendulum's precession, and it is why the commutation failure is intrinsically geometric rather than being due to the coordinate system or numerical grid. A recently proposed generalized spherical convolution is, for a given scalar kernel, the unique linear operator commuting with the radial projection, divergence, and curl. Any consistent linear operator, be it spectral truncation, wavelet transform, diffusion, Green's-function inversion, or a machine-learned convolution, necessarily takes this form. From a simulation of an unstable jet, we demonstrate commutation to within numerical round-off, whereas common filtering that ignores curvature produces significant spurious divergence where none exists and gradient errors comparable to the gradients themselves.

title: Transverse Confinement in Cascaded Inverse-Cherenkov Acceleration via Phase-Trajectory Control and Injection Matching
abstract: Sub-relativistic electrons in micron-scale dielectric laser accelerators face coupled challenges of longitudinal dephasing and transverse defocusing, often imposing stringent requirements on injector emittance. Here, we demonstrate a combined strategy of phase-trajectory control and injection matching for sustained, confined acceleration. By coordinating the refractive-index and section-length sequences with the injected beam's Twiss parameters, we control accumulated phase slippage while maintaining transverse confinement. In a seven-section inverse-Cherenkov accelerator simulation, a 100-keV electron bunch with an initial normalized transverse emittance of 1 nm-rad and a relative kinetic-energy spread of 0.1% reaches 1154.7 keV over 1.545 mm, with a transverse rms beam size below 1 $μ$m throughout the accelerating channels. The exit normalized emittance is 1.92 nm-rad, and the relative RMS kinetic-energy spread is 0.6%, with no particle loss under the specified tracking-acceptance criterion. The results demonstrate that coordinated structural sequencing and injection matching can relax injector-emittance requirements by up to approximately two orders of magnitude, offering a route toward compact dielectric accelerators for ultrafast electron diffraction, microscopy, and chip-scale coherent radiation.

title: Decay of space plasma turbulence downstream of bow shocks: MMS magnetosheath unbiased campaign observations
abstract: Turbulence properties in the solar wind change with increasing heliospheric distance. Observations from different missions have shown how spectral indices converge towards a $f^{-5/3}$ spectrum in the inertial range as the solar wind reaches one astronomical unit, and how the cascade rate decays as the plasma moves away from the Sun. We evaluate whether these properties display similar trends in a smaller astrophysical system, that of a planetary magnetosheath. Using data from the 2023 Magnetospheric Multiscale (MMS) unbiased magnetosheath campaign, we determine the evolution of the spectral indices and the cascade rate along 15 inbound magnetosheath crossings. WIND observations permitted to monitor the state of the solar wind during the campaign and allowed to study the impact of the upstream plasma conditions on the evolution of the cascade rate downstream the bow shock. Our results show an increase of the cascade rate between two to three orders of magnitude after the plasma crosses the bow shock into the magnetosheath. Once in the magnetosheath, turbulence develops with increasing distance to the bow shock in a way similar to solar wind observations, despite the smaller size of the system. Incompressible Hall-MHD scaling-law estimates of the cascade rate show a clear power-law decay of the cascade rate in the magnetosheath, particularly for the cases with upstream slow wind. This suggests that the way energy is injected into the system plays a role in the decay of turbulence as the plasma moves away from the bow shock.

title: Solar Magnetic Configuration Control over Radiation Belt Electrons
abstract: Earth is surrounded by two highly dynamic concentric belts of particle radiation. The outer radiation belt exhibits coherent variability at solar-cycle, seasonal, and 27-day (Carrington) timescales. While the solar-cycle and Carrington variations have been attributed to the recurrence of coronal hole solar wind, the seasonal variation has long been explained by local geometric effects that modulate the solar wind-magnetosphere coupling. Here, we challenge this paradigm by showing that the periodic recurrence of coronal hole solar wind likewise drives the seasonal variation. We further demonstrate that the Alfvénic nature of this solar wind is a key driver of the observed electron flux enhancement in the outer radiation belt. These findings provide a unifying framework linking solar magnetic topology, solar wind properties, and magnetospheric dynamics across multiple timescales at Earth and beyond.
